facility
1 Interest only payment Only interest is paid on the loan and no principal repayment
(only allowed for is made. The principal amount remains unchanged and the
maximum up to period terms for the repayment structure are reassessed at the end of

ability.
2 payment moratorium An agreement allowing the borrower a defined delay in

3 Capitalization Addition of those unpaid amounts (interest and late fees) to
the principal balance for repayment under a sustainable
rescheduled programme.
4 Extension of maturity Extension of the maturity of the loan which allows a
term/ rescheduling reduction in installment amounts by spreading the

4. Foreclosure of Non-Performing Loans
4.1. Pre-litigation Foreclosure
a. When a loan account becomes or shows signs of account becoming NPL such as loans
overdue by more than 30 days or behind an agreed schedule of payment or any events that
will likely impair the borrower’s repayment capacity, the FSP shall follow up with the
borrower to upgrade or maintain the account as performing. Depending on the nature of
the NPL, the recovery process shall be carried out as per FSP’s policies, procedures and
manuals which should be in line with the following:
i. Section 3 of these regulations;
ii. Out of Court Settlement (Refer Appendix A)
iii. Tracing untraceable NPL borrowers (Refer Appendix B); or
iv. Any other relevant directives issued by the Authority from time to time.
b. An FSP shall ensure all follow-ups and negotiations with a borrower are properly
documented with supporting evidence.
c. If a borrower fails to upgrade the NPL to a performing status through the follow-up and
negotiation the FSP shall initiate foreclosure process for the recovery of the loan
outstanding.
d. An FSP shall review and verify the loan documents for any issue of cross-collateralization,
secondary charges, paripasu charges against the collateral/mortgage or when the borrower
is a common borrower among the FSPs. If any issue arises from Section 3.1. (c) above, the
same shall be resolved between the FSP and borrower before moving forward to the next
step.
e. An FSP and non-willful defaulter may choose to enter into negotiation for:
i. Voluntary surrender of the loan security by the borrower for full or partial
settlement of the loan outstanding;
ii. Both the FSP and borrower shall have the right to enter into negotiation for
voluntary surrender or takeover of the loan collateral/mortgage
iii. In the event FSP agrees to accept the security for full settlement of the loan
outstanding, the FSP shall enter into a negotiated settlement with the

borrower/mortgagor and proceed to foreclose the NPL and the NPL account shall
be closed after taking over of the property; and/or
iv. Transfer the NPL to a third party by taking over the security or business from the
borrower.
f. The FSP shall freeze the interest once the physical possession of the loan
collateral/mortgage is taken over by the FSP or based on the court order.
4.2. Foreclosure through Court
a. When an FSP does not foresee any viability to reach a settlement through a negotiation
with the borrower during the pre-litigation foreclosure, an FSP shall initiate recovery
proceedings in the court of law for the foreclosure of collateral/mortgage within 365 Days
Past Due. However, for small-ticket loans, foreclosure through the court may not be
required if a cost-benefit analysis justifies such an approach. The FSP shall adopt a Board-
approved internal policy that specifies the threshold loan amount or outstanding balance
below which court-based foreclosure is not mandatory. In line with this policy, the FSP
may proceed with writing off the loan, waiving the outstanding amount, or taking any other
action, it deems appropriate.
b. An FSP shall stipulate the timeline in its Guidelines within which a recovery suit shall be
filed against the NPL borrower.
c. During the judicial proceedings if a borrower pleads before the court for out-of-court
settlement through negotiation, an FSP may, with the leave of the court, negotiate with the
borrower for the foreclosure of the NPL in question.
d. If a borrower is untraceable for a period of three months despite all reasonable efforts as
per their SoP and the FSP is not able to resolve at its level, the FSP may register cases
against the borrower and request the court to issue a summon order, direct to carry out the
announcement in the media and issue arrest warrants against the untraceable borrower as
per the procedures of the court.
e. If a borrower is still untraceable after exhausting the steps stipulated under Section 4.2.(d),
the FSP may, within a period of one month, request the court to declare the borrower
missing and issue default judgment for the FSP to take over the collateral/mortgage or to
enforce the rights of the FSP to claim its loan outstanding.

6. Write-off of NPLs
6.1. General Process
a. Write-off means removing NPLs from the balance sheet by taking a charge against the
profit and loss account of the FSPs.
b. The loans written-off shall be recorded as an off-balance sheet and FSPs shall continue to
pursue recovery or closure of the NPL.
c. A loan write-off does not forfeit the legal right of the FSPs to recover its loan outstanding
in the future.
d. All loans that have been 100% provisioned and in loss category (loan default by more than
365 days) may be written-off from the balance sheet of FSPs as per the internal policies of
FSP approved by their board.
e. FSP shall write-off the loans only after the commencement of foreclosure through court.
f. The interest and late fees as per the loan agreement shall continue to accrue on the loans
written-off. The FSPs may compute interest and late fee at the end during the loan
recovery/closure.
g. The FSPs shall maintain a proper record and all the relevant documentary evidence of the
written-off loans.
h. The FSPs shall form a dedicated Recovery Unit/Division/assign to existing divisions to
pursue recovery of the written-off loans with clear strategy and targets set by Management
and approved by their Board.
i. The FSPs shall continue submitting the details of the loan written-off to the Credit
Information Bureau (CIB) until the loan outstanding is liquidated/closed.
j. The FSP shall submit a detailed report on the loans written-off to the Authority for
information as part of existing monthly returns.
k. The FSP shall maintain proper internal controls and oversight to ensure that the operational
risk such as process of write-off under these regulations are carried out prudently.
l. The FSP is required to ensure that the loans written off are properly audited by the internal
auditors and the statutory auditors and disclosed in the annual report.

7.1. Non-Performing Loan (NPL): means the loan repayment obligations which are overdue

The non-performing loans includes following features:
a. Role of collateralization: Collateralization or guarantees shall have no direct influence
on the categorization of loan as non-performing.
b. Upgrading to performing: The criteria for reclassifying a non-performing loan as
performing, under the determination of non-performing exposures, shall conform to the
applicable legal framework established by the authority.
7.2. Absconded: Absconded means a person who had left or abandoned the country without
the knowledge of the Royal Government for reasons of corruption charges either due to
corrupt reasons or after having committed anti-national activities or the crime against the
State or Tsawa Sum with sole intent for avoiding judicial process, and whose census has
been deleted from the RGoB records based on the reports of respective local governments.
The final list of absconded borrowers shall be confirmed in writing by the Department of
Law & Order, MoHCA to the FSPs and Authority.
7.3. Authority: means as defined in the RMA Act of Bhutan 2010 or amendment thereof.
7.4. Collateral or mortgage: means movable and immovable properties pledged as the security
against loans as stipulated in the Movable and Immovable Property Act of Bhutan 1999 or

7.5. Financial Service Providers (FSPs): means an individual or an entity who/which is given
the registration certificates or licenses by the Authority to provide the financial services to

7.6. Foreclosure: means a legal process by which an FSP attempts to recover or liquidate the

through out-of-court settlement in full or partial settlement of the NPLs as approved by the
Boards of FSPs.
7.7. Out-of-Court Settlement: means an agreement between FSPs and borrowers to amicably

identify asset quality problems early on through clean balance sheets.
2. Definition & Treatment
2.1. In line with Section 6, write-off is only an accounting term for derecognition/ removal
of the NPLs from the books (balance sheet) of the FSPs and transfer it to off-balance

2.2. To ensure that the term “write- off” does not confuse oversight authorities and the
public as different authorities have different interpretations/ of the term, the RMA will

2.3. A charge-off does not preclude the FSP from enforcing and recovering the debt

which are exposures that could impact the books of the FSPs in the future based on the
possibility/occurrence of an event. For example, the recovery of loans charged-off will

2.5. Off-balance sheet exposures include bank guarantees, letter of credit, loans charged-off
or any other contingent assets or liabilities as per BAS 37 Provisions, Contingent Assets
and Contingent Liabilities.

Appendix B: SOP on Out of Court Settlement
1. Background
The out-of-court settlement is being designed for FSPs and loan defaulters to amicably resolve the
existing NPLs through the out-of-court settlement for expediting the NPL resolution with the
objective to relieve borrowers and strengthen the capital and liquidity of the FSPs to prepare for
risks in the future.
Out-of-court settlement (hereafter OCS) is an agreement between FSPs and borrowers to amicably
resolve the NPLs without going to court as litigations are costly and time consuming and waste
resources for both the parties.
Current practices highlight that the borrowers and FSPs still prefer to litigate through court for
foreclosure of NPLs since both the parties do not have incentive to reach the OCS. Therefore, the
standard operating procedures for the OCS is being issued to provide a standard framework for
borrowers and FSPs to amicably resolve the NPLs through OCS.
2. Objectives and Eligibility
2.1. The objectives of this SOPs are to:
a. Provide framework to FSPs for the out-of-court settlement of NPLs.
b. Encourage borrowers and FSPs to amicably resolve the NPLs; and
c. Relieve borrowers from debt burden and strengthen capital position of FSPs through
fast recovery process of NPLs.
2.2. The following categories of NPLs shall be eligible for the OCS:
a. All NPLs parked under the Asset Pending Foreclosure as per Guidelines on Transfer
of NPL Asset, 2020;
b. Any NPLs that have been transferred off-balance sheet for decongesting the books of
accounts;
c. Any NPLs whereby the securities have been seized by the FSPs as per the provisions
of MIPA 1999; and
d. Any other category specified by the Authority from time to time.
2.3. The following NPLs shall not be eligible for OCS:
a. Government/Ministry guaranteed loans;
Page 26 of 33

b. Employee incentive loans; Willful defaulters as per the Guidelines on Segregation of
NPLs into Viable and Non-viable Loans 2021; and
c. Any other category specified by the Authority from time to time.
3. Modality
3.1. The FSPs shall determine the following factors for designing the OCS:
a. The FSP shall review the loan documents and revalue the loan securities to determine
the `MRA" (Maximum Recoverability Amount).
b. The FSP shall break down the total loan outstanding into principal balance, interest
outstanding and late fee/penalty accrued.
c. The FSPs shall compare the MRA and total loan outstanding for settlement of the
NPLs.
d. The portion of total loan outstanding, which is greater than the MRA, the FSPs may
choose to partially write-off the loans to resolve the NPLs through OCS.
3.2. Based on the institution specific NPL experience, the FSPs can design the OCS schemes
as per the following modalities:
a. Option 1: Settlement through liquidation of account
The FSPs shall enter the OCS for liquidation of NPL accounts through repayment by
the client.
b. Option 2: Debt-to-asset swap
The FSPs and borrowers may enter into voluntary surrender agreement of properties
for complete or partial settlement of loan with partial write-off of interest accrued and
late fees to encourage/incentivize OCS. However, if MRA can not cover substantial
part of total loan outstanding under this option, the FSPs may restructure the loan
balance after settlement, with submission of new securities and new execution of loan
agreement between the FSP and the borrower.
4. Accounting and Prudential requirements
4.1. The FSPs shall write-back the provisions of the recovered portion under OCS through
profit and loss accounts or income statement.
Page 27 of 33

4.2. Any partial write-offs shall be adjusted against the existing provisions or interest-in-
suspense kept aside for the NPL account.
4.3. In case the provisions or interest-in-suspense is not adequate to cover the partial write-
offs, the difference shall directly be expensed through profit and loss accounts or income
statement.
4.4. Asset taken over will be booked as "foreclosed assets" under "other assets".
4.5. Any restructured loans from Option 2: Debt-Asset Swap shall be under probation for 6
months before classifying the account as standard.
4.6. The borrower availing OCS scheme shall have settlement history in the CIB report.
5. Implementation
5.1. The FSP shall design their own OCS schemes according to the institution specific NPL
issues and notify RMA with prior approval of their Board.
5.2. The FSP shall provide monthly update on OCS implementation to Authority.
5.3. FSP to train their staffs and prepare for the OCS implementation.
5.4. Any deviation from the SoP issued by Authority shall require prior approval of Authority
through the individual institutions' Boards.
5.5. The FSP shall design FAQs/clarifications to have clear understanding by the borrowers
to facilitate smooth operation of the scheme.
5.6. The OCS facility shall be provided to all eligible borrowers and no favored terms shall
be given to any borrowers.
Page 28 of 33

Appendix C: SOP on tracing untraceable NPL borrowers
1. Background
In line with the resolution adopted during the second National High-Level Committee meeting
held on 3rd February 2021 for the resolution of non-performing loans, the Standard Operating
Procedure (SOP) is being issued to assist the Financial Service Providers in tracing the untraceable
borrowers with non-performing loan accounts and treatment of NPLs thereof.
2. Untraceable Borrower
2.1. As per Guidelines on Foreclosure and Write Off of NPLs, an Untraceable/missing borrower
means a borrower who has been at large and the FSP ’s recovery procedure has been fully
exhausted (through media announcement, issue of arrest warrant by the Court and the
police has confirmed in writing that the said borrower is untraceable/missing from Bhutan).
The respective Boards of FSPs shall confirm and approve the final list of
untraceable/missing borrowers and share the same with the RMA.
2.2. Considering the present issues of untraceable borrower at different levels such as arrest
warrant issued by the court or still in process being tracked by the Financial Institutions,
the SOP is developed with the intent to provide a uniform approach in tracing the borrowers
within the existing legal framework and address the NPLs arising from such issues.
3. Different Level of Tracing the borrower
3.1. Level 1: Tracing the borrower at Financial Institution level
a. As and when the loan account becomes NPL or is behind the agreed repayment
schedule as per the terms and conditions of Loan Agreement, the FSPs shall follow
up with borrowers for loan repayment.
b. If the borrower cannot be located or contacted due to change in contact address and
contact number, the FSPs shall carry out the following to confirm the borrower’s
whereabouts:
i. Contact witness/s who have signed on the loan documents;
ii. Contact local government/s; and
Page 29 of 33

iii. Request family contact details from Department of Civil Registration and
Census, MOHCA.
c. The FSPs shall document and maintain record specified under 9.3.2.
3.2. Level 2: Tracing the borrower through the court’s intervention
a. If FSPs are still not able to trace the borrowers through the steps stipulated under
Level 1, the FSPs shall request legal interventions from the court/s.
b. The FSPs shall submit the written documents as evidence to substantiate that the
FSPs has exhausted all steps from Level 1, to the court/s.
c. The FSPs shall request the intervention from the court/s to locate or trace the
borrower through issue of court order for the following:
i. Requesting mobile numbers from telecommunication service providers based on
CID; and
ii. Media announcement of asking clients to report to Financial Institutions and the
media expense will be borne by the FIs.
d. If the borrower fails to report as per steps in 9.4.3, the FSPs shall request court/s to
issue arrest warrant against the borrower.
3.3 Level 3: Declaring the borrower as missing/untraceable
If FSPs are still not able to locate or contact the borrowers through the interventions from Level 2,
then the Financial Institution shall request the court/s to declare the borrower as missing and
request court to allow FSPs to register case for default judgement to take over the mortgaged
properties or enforce the rights of the FSP when the borrower is found.
3.3. Transfer of NPL Asset, write-off and accounting treatment
a. Once the borrower has been declared missing, the FSP shall write-off the NPLs as
per these regulations.
b. The FSPs shall take note that write-off means only removing bad loans from the
books of accounts and shall not entail in forgiveness of debt as per these regulations.
c. The accounting treatment for write-offs shall be in line these regulations.
Page 30 of 33

Appendix D: Documentation of restructured Loans
1. Retail borrowers
1.1. An FSP shall consider the following information wherever applicable to assess the
borrower’s affordability of availing the loan restructuring facility:
a. Assessment of the borrower’s current and future repayment ability.
Information to consider for current repayment Information to consider for future repayment
ability ability
 financial information (occupation, income,  income
expenditure)  years to retirement (in comparison to loan
 overall loan exposure duration)
 current repayment capacity  employment status or prospects
 repayment history  industry/ sector
 reason for arrears  savings and assets
 age and amount of arrear  known future changes
 Alternative/secondary repayment source
(family members)
b. Affordability assessment of guarantors (if applicable).
1.2. As a minimum, the following documents should be obtained when restructuring a retail
loan:
a. Written application from the borrower requesting for loan restructuring facility
indicating reasons for financial hardship;
b. Financial and non-financial information of a borrower (e.g. pay slips or tax returns
for salary and rental incomes, tax returns for formal business entities with licenses
and for informal business, any supporting documents demonstrating the borrower’s
income and ability to service the loan obligations.
c. Recent CIB report; Latest valuation of collateral/ mortgage securing the underlying
loan facility;
Page 31 of 33

d. Information on any other collateral securing the underlying loan facilities (e.g.
insurance, third party guarantees); and
e. Any other document required by FSPs depending on the requirement of the
assessment.
f. Letter of undertaking in case of alternative/secondary source of repayment
g. Any other document required by FSPs on a case to case basis.
2. Corporate borrowers
2.1. In case of a corporate borrower, an FSP shall consider the following information wherever
applicable to assess the borrower’s affordability of availing the loan restructuring facility:
a. Overall loan exposure
b. Analysis/assessment of the company’s business plan (e.g. SWOT analysis,
projected financial ratio analysis, industry sector analysis);
c. Company’s history on financial data, which may help trace the trigger event of the
company experiencing difficulties and may provide an indication as to the viability
of its business model;
d. Business model/business activity of the borrower or the economic environment
both past and future;
e. Scrutiny and assessment for reasonableness of projections and assumptions;
f. Analysis of current obligations (major expenses, capital expenditure, disposals,
equity contribution, other amounts due (fines, taxes, insurance, employee
liabilities) etc.;
g. Affordability assessment of guarantors (if applicable);
h. Industry and sector analysis; and
i. Relevant market indicators.
2.2. As a minimum, the following documents shall be obtained as evidence when restructuring
a corporate loan:
a. Written application from the borrower requesting loan restructuring facility
indicating reasons for financial hardship;
b. Latest audited financial statements and/or latest management accounts;
c. Recent CIB report;
Page 32 of 33

d. Business plan and/or cash-flow forecast, depending on the size of the borrower and
the maturity of the loan;
e. Latest valuation report of any collateral/mortgage securing the underlying loan; and
f. Information on any other collateral securing the underlying loan facilities (e.g,
insurance).

PART 1. PRELIMINARY
1.1 Introduction
Stress testing is a quantitative technique to measure the impact on a financial institution or
system in the event of exceptional but plausible incidents. Macro stress testing, as a methodology
of macroprudential analysis for assessing system risk as part of a financial stability supervisory
role, is widely used to evaluate financial stability in the event of exogenous shocks.
Since the global financial crisis (GFC), stress testing has become a well-established regulatory
tool to assess the resilience of the financial sector (Baudino, et al., 2018). Stress tests offer
quantitative, forward-looking evaluations of the financial system’s health and solvency under
various plausible scenarios. These tests can be designed with either a micro-prudential or
macroprudential policy focus. Macro stress tests, in particular, assess the financial system's
resilience using an adverse macroeconomic scenario that incorporates multiple risk factors. This
contrasts with sensitivity analysis, which examines the impact of specific risk factors in isolation,
without considering their interactions within the broader financial system.
Next to the prime responsibility of monetary policy, the responsibility to safeguard financial
stability features prominently in the mandate of the RMA. Therefore, DFRS has developed a
macro stress testing framework that will be used regularly for forward-looking financial
institution solvency assessments. Moreover, the importance of stress within the RMA is
reinforced by Risk Based Supervision, which requires tools to identify vulnerable financial
institutions both at a bank or non-bank level (micro-prudential) and a system-wide
(macro-prudential) perspective.
1.2 Objectives
The macro stress testing framework will be a policy toolkit to assess the resilience of Bhutan’s
financial system to adverse economic shocks by identifying systemic risks, evaluating their
potential impact, and supporting macro-prudential policy decisions. It helps strengthen financial
stability by integrating macro-financial linkages, enhancing data-driven risk assessment, and
ensuring effective regulatory oversight.
Page | 1

1.3 Scope
This stress testing framework is expected to be used for both top-down stress testing by
supervisors and bottom-up stress testing by financial institutions. These stress tests shall be
conducted under different macroeconomic scenarios designed by the supervisor. The top-down
stress testing conducted by the supervisor will project the stress test results using a set of
supervisory models that take as inputs bank-provided data on financial condition and risk
characteristics, as well as the supervisory scenarios. The stress test uses models developed or
selected by the supervisor, which may be refined each year in advance of the stress test. The
framework assesses various risk dimensions, including credit, market, liquidity, and operational
risks. Macro stress testing will be conducted over different time horizons, covering short-term
(six months to one year) and medium-term (one to three years) projections. The stress testing
will be conducted annually or depends on regulatory requirements.
1.4 Commencement
This framework shall:
(a) Be called “A Macro Stress Testing Framework for Solvency Assessment, 2025”;
(b) Come into force from 1st July 2025;
1.5 Score of Application
Apply to all the Financial Service Providers licensed/registered as per the FSA 2011.
Page | 2

PART 2. METHODOLOGY: FRAMEWORK
The proposed stress testing framework will use a structured, modular approach to assess the
resilience of financial institutions under adverse macroeconomic conditions. This framework is
adapted from the European Central Bank’s (ECB) solvency analysis, consisting of four
interrelated analytical pillars as shown in the figure below.
The first pillar (scenario design) entails creating macro-financial scenarios that will be applied to
the financial sector. These
scenarios include baseline and
adverse conditions, and take into
account key economic variables
such as GDP growth, inflation,
interest rates, and exchange rate
variations. The purpose is to
model probable financial stress
and assess how banks might
behave in various economic scenarios. The second pillar (top-down satellite models) consists of
models that translate macroeconomic scenarios into financial variables that directly affect
financial institutions' balance sheets. The third pillar (balance sheet) integrates the projected
models into individual financial institution balance sheets. This step allows for the calculation of
the impact on the solvency position of the financial institution, including capital adequacy and
risk-weighted asset changes. Finally, the fourth pillar (feedback) extends the analysis beyond the
initial impact on capital to assess second round effects. This includes evaluating the potential
contagion risk with the financial system and broader feedback loops to the real economy, such as
changes in credit supply and economic activity.
Page | 3

2.1 Macro-Financial Scenario Design
The objective of stress testing is to analyse the impact of potential shocks to the economy and
financial institutions. Based on one or more of the risk factors identified in the Financial
Stability reports, the scenarios will vary over time. In financial system oversight, risk factors
that are highly improbable but have serious repercussions for the economy and the financial
sector can easily be overlooked. Stress scenarios, therefore, apply shocks that would have
severe adverse consequences if they were to occur. The depth of scenarios, i.e., how severe
they are, will vary as a consequence of changes in the risk factors. At the same time,
projections for the baseline scenario and the uncertainty surrounding these projections will
have an impact on stress scenarios. In a downturn where economic developments are highly
uncertain and where risk factors can have serious consequences, the impact shown in the
stress test may be considerable.
(a) Macroeconomic Block
(i) The general starting point for any stress testing exercise, be it top-down or
bottom-up, is a set of macro-financial risks that could have a bearing on the
resilience of the banking system. Under this framework, the identification and
monitoring of systemic risks will be derived from its financial stability
surveillance exercises. The approach of mapping risks to scenarios should be
characterized by following important elements:
(ii) The scenarios should reflect severe but plausible outcomes, ensuring a level of
severity that significantly impacts banks while remaining realistic. This is
typically defined in probabilistic terms, considering both initial shocks (e.g.,
ROA or ROI changes) and their effects on key macroeconomic variables (e.g.,
GDP growth).
(iii) Macroeconomic scenarios for unemployment, GDP growth, land and building
valuation, inflation and monetary policy are generated exogenously using the
macro models. These scenarios are input as conditional assumption paths into a
reduced form of conditional satellite models to forecast credit risk, market risk
and profit model.
Page | 4

(iv) These scenarios should interact with the satellite models at the financial
institution level block, influencing the balance sheet and profit and loss accounts
across individual financial institutions. This process should generate paths for
Tier 1 capital resulting from the realization of the input macroeconomic
scenarios for the first year of the model run.
(v) The derived path for Tier 1 from the financial institution level block should be
used to calibrate a capital deleveraging shock in a structural Vector
Autoregression (SVAR) model (Refer Appendix A).
Figure 2 Scenario generation process
2.2 Financial Institution Level Block
The financial institution level block consists of two modules, Satellite models and Balance sheet.
The Satellite models comprises three main models: credit risk model, profit model and market
risk model. Beside three main models, the liquidity stress indicators should constitute an inherent
part of the solvency stress testing framework (Macro stress testing framework). These liquidity
stress indicators should be used from the liquidity stress testing framework, in the form of market
liquidity (the risk that an asset can not be sold or used as collateral) or funding liquidity (the risk
that financial institutions are unable to roll-over maturity funding).
Page | 5

The credit risk model and profit model should impact the profit and loss account through
impairments and net interest income, respectively, and ultimately capital through retained
earnings in the capital account. The credit risk models should use the credit parameters such as
probability of default (PD), Loss Given Default (LGD) and Exposure at Default to obtain the
estimate for expected credit losses over the scenario horizon. The assumptions and projections
from the satellite modules are translated into revenues, expenses, losses and provisions. Further,
the profit model should translate projections on interest rates and assumptions on balance sheet
growth into interest income and expense. The approach can be divided into four modules: the net
interest income calculation, the loan losses and impairment calculation, the market risk
calculation and the final profit and loss calculation. Under the balance sheet module, it should
calculate interest income and interest expenses dependent on the macro scenario projections.
Figure 3 Profit and Loss Calculation Process
At the macro level, financial institution level capital depletion will be aggregated to estimate the
impact on the system-wide capital position for a given macroeconomic projection. The solvency
calculation should comprise of the definition and calculation method of capital, which includes
net income and Total Risk Weighted Assets (RWA). Therefore, solvency ratio is calculated as the
sum of the existing capital stock and earnings accumulated over the stress period in relation to
Page | 6

the end-horizon risk-weighted assets, as shown in figure 4. The composition of capital should be
aligned with the standard definition set by the regulator.
Figure 4 Solvency Calculation Process
2.3 Feedback Analysis
Macro stress test exercises typically end once the first-round impact on the stressed financial
institutions’ solvency position is derived. However, in reality it is to be expected that banks
would react to stressed situations by adjusting their balance sheets in certain ways, which in turn
could have ramifications on the real economy and on other banks in the system. To analyse such
effects, financial network analysis tools should be applied. Such actions, for example in the form
of loan supply restrictions, could be expected to have real economic implications which would
tend to amplify the original adverse macroeconomic scenario. To account for such feedback
effects linking results from the stress testing framework to the broader economy requires
macroeconomic models with financial sector interfaces that can derive the macroeconomic
implications of shocks hitting the financial sector.
Page | 7

1. PRELIMINARY
1.1 Objectives
The primary objective of this framework is to supplement and facilitate the enforcement of Section
3 of the Prudential Regulation 2024, and Sections 234 - 241 of the Financial Services Act 2011.
This framework establishes maximum limits and prudential requirements for the regulatory
oversight of financial institutions' exposures to a single counterparty or a group of connected
counterparties.
1.2 Title, Commencement and Application
This framework shall
(a) be called the Large Exposure Framework, hereafter referred to as LEF 2025.
(b) come into effect from 1st July 2025
(c) apply to all FIs regulated by the Royal Monetary Authority
(d) be reviewed and amended from time to time.
2. LARGE EXPOSURE
2.1 Definition
Large exposures shall mean those exposures of a FIs to an individual borrower or a group of
connected borrowers, which is equal to or more than 10 percent of the Tier I capital based on the
latest audited balance sheet.
2.2 Computation of large exposure
As stated in section 3.2.2 of PR 2024, the FIs shall consider the following to compute large
exposures:
(a) Term loan: outstanding balance
(b) Overdraft facilities: sanction amount or outstanding balance whichever is higher
(c) Off-balance sheet items: off-balance amount less margin money
Page 1 of 6

2.3 Maximum limit on large exposures
(a) Exposures to any single company, public corporation, firm, association of persons, or an
individual shall not exceed 25 percent of the FI’s Tier I capital in line with section 3.4.4(i) of
PR 2024
(b) The following exposure shall be aggregated and shall not exceed 30 percent of the Tier 1
Capital in line with section 3.4.4(ii) of PR 2024.
i. an individual, his close relations or a company or firm in which he or his close relations
have a substantial interest; or,
ii. a group of connected borrowers if at least one of the following criteria is satisfied:
1. Control relationship: in assessing whether there is a control relationship between
counterparties, financial institutions must consider these criteria if one entity owns
more than 10% (significant owner) of the shareholding of the other entity. In addition,
financial institutions must assess connectedness between counterparties based on
control using the following criteria:
(a) is able to appoint or remove the majority of board of directors or management of
the other;
(b) is able to cast the majority of votes at meetings of the board, general meeting or
equivalent governing body of the other;
(c) is able to direct the activities of the other so as to obtain benefits from its activities;
and
(d) commonality of ownership and management
2. Economic interdependence: in establishing connectedness based on economic
interdependence, FIs shall consider, at a minimum, the following criteria:
(a) having the same expected source of repayments
Page 2 of 6

(b) an individual, his/her spouse and economically dependent children;
(c) where one counterparty has fully or partly guaranteed the exposure of the other
counterparty;
(d) where it is likely that the financial problems of one counterparty would cause
difficulties for the other counterparty in terms of full and timely repayment of loan
liabilities
(e) where the insolvency or default of one counterparty is likely to be associated with
the Insolvency or default of the other; and
(f) significant association or relationship exists among counterparties, e.g. sharing of
common marketing and/or branding platform etc.
2.4. Disaggregation of exposures
In line with section 3.3.4 of PR 2024, a FIs may disaggregate its exposures for computation of
the large exposures limit if the following criteria are met:
(a) a single borrower or such connected person has sufficient financial resources of its own to
obtain credit facilities and to fully service its liabilities; and
(b) a single borrower or such connected person is not relied upon to support the liabilities of the
other or other persons connected to the counterparty out of its financial resources.
2.5. Exclusions of exposures
In line with section 3.4.5 of PR 2024, the following exposures shall be excluded from the
computation of large exposures:
(a) inter-bank exposures with a maturity of three months or less;
(b) exposures fully covered by cash collateral;
(c) exposures covered by government guarantees;
(d) exposures to governments and the central banks.
Page 3 of 6

2.6. Maximum limit on total large exposures
In line with section 239 of FSA 2011, the sum of its large exposures shall not exceed 8 times of
Tier 1 capital.
2.7. Prudent requirement
In pursuant to section 3.8 of PR 2024 on the general requirement, the policy on large exposure
shall include the following but not limited to:
(a) Internal Risk Appetite
Defining risk appetite to align their risk exposure with their financial capacity and strategic
objectives, preventing excessive risk-taking.
(b) Internal Risk Tolerance limit
Clear risk tolerance thresholds for not exceeding acceptable risk levels, safeguarding against
potential financial instability from large exposures.
(c) Early Warning System
An early warning system to provide prompt detection of emerging risks, allowing timely
intervention before issues escalate into significant losses.
(d) Escalation Process
A defined escalation process to ensure critical risks are promptly communicated to senior
management and the Board for swift decision-making and action.
(e) Risk Mitigation Plan
i. A risk mitigation plan to outline strategies to reduce potential risks, ensuring the institution
is prepared to manage and minimize adverse impacts from large exposure.
ii. As required by section 114(i) of CGRR 2024, the large exposures must be reviewed by the
Risk Management Function
iii. As required by section 127 of CGRR 2024, the large exposure must be audited by the
internal audit every quarter and submit the report to the Authority also in line with section
3.4 (iv) of PR 2024 to ensure compliance to the prudential limit and standards/internal
policies;
Page 4 of 6

iv. The FIs shall conduct stress tests and scenario analyses to determine how their large
exposures will perform under adverse economic conditions to prepare for unexpected
shocks.
v. As per section 240 of FSA 2011, FIs will report to Authority within 7 days risk after
reaching the risk tolerance limit.
vi. A financial institution that fails to comply with any of these regulations, shall be liable to
the penalties in line with section 241 FSA 2011, Thus, Non-compliance shall be fined as
per the Penalty Rules and Regulations 2022 and amendment thereof
vii. Additionally, FIs shall assign risk weight of l50% for capital adequacy computations in the
event of the exposures exceeding the maximum limits
3. OTHER REQUIREMENTS
3.1. Regulatory reporting and monitoring
(a) FIs shall submit the report to authority on large exposures on a monthly basis as per the Annex
I.
(b) The Authority shall monitor the adherence to the provisions of the framework through its
regular on-site- inspection and off-site surveillance of the regulated entities;
(c) The Authority shall take supervisory actions against the regulated entities' non-compliance
with these Guidelines.

CHAPTER 1: PRELIMINARIES
1.1. Authority
In exercising the powers conferred to the Royal Monetary Authority of Bhutan (hereinafter
referred to as "the Authority") under Section 167 and 171 of the Financial Services Act 2011, the
Board of the Authority hereby adopts the Penalty (Amendment) Regulations.These regulations
establish the principles and methodologies for determining and imposing administrative penalties
on any individuals or Financial Services Providers (hereinafter referred to as “FSPs”) that violate
any provisions of the rules, regulations, guidelines, directives, and notifications issued by the
Authority from time to time.
1.2. Scope and Objective
The Authority plays a critical role in maintaining the safety, soundness, and stability of the
financial system in the interest of the nation. To fulfill this mandate, the Authority shall take
timely and appropriate action against any individuals or FSPs that fail to comply with the
regulatory requirements.
The objective of these regulations is to provide broad provisions for assessing and
imposing monetary and administrative penalties, mainly to:
a) reinforce the integrity and credibility of FSPs by ensuring that violations are
swiftly identified, strictly monitored, and penalized with severity commensurate to
the breach;
b) guarantee that enforcement actions are not only proportionate but also firm,
predictable, and uniformly applied; and
c) deter individuals and FSPs from contravening any rules, regulations, guidelines,
directives, and notifications, issued by the Authority.
1.3. Title, Commencement, and Application
This Regulations shall:
(a) Be called the Penalty (Amendment) Regulations 2025;
(b) Come into force from July 2025 and;
(c) Shall apply to:
i. All the FSPs licensed, registered, or authorized by the Authority.
ii. Any individual who is governed by regulations which are framed and enforced
by the Authority.
3

1.4. Repeal and Saving
Upon adoption of the amended regulations by the Board of the Authority:
(a) The Penalty Rules and Regulations 2022 shall stand repealed;
(b) Supersede any directive, circular, guidelines, references or notifications that are
inconsistent with these regulations; and
(c) All actions taken by the Authority under the Penalty Rules and Regulations 2022
shall stand until appropriate remedies or rectifications are carried out by the FSPs.
1.5. Interpretation
The Authority shall interpret any provision of these regulations, and its interpretation shall
be final and binding on any individuals or FSPs.
CHAPTER 2: VIOLATIONS AND PROCEDURES FOR DETERMINING
ADMINISTRATIVE SANCTIONS OR MONETARY PENALTIES
2.1. Violations
The Authority shall consider violations eligible for monetary penalties and/or
administrative sanctions including, but not limited to, the following:
(a) Violation of the rules, regulations, guidelines, or directives issued by the Authority;
(b) Non-compliance with the observations/findings/corrective actions within the
timeline prescribed by the Authority;
(c) Contraventions that are tantamount to offence and not covered by these regulations;
and
(d) Notwithstanding the above provisions, offences that are clearly stipulated with a
penalty in the Acts shall be dealt with as per the provisions of the respective Acts.
2.2. Penalty Assessment Criteria
In determining the monetary penalty, the Authority must consider a wide range of factors to
ensure that it arrives at a fair and proportionate amount that reflects the gravity of the
violation and the circumstances of each case. The factors include, but are not limited, to the
following:
(a) Severity of the violation(s);
(b) Intent and negligence;
(c) Frequency of violations;
(d) Remedial actions taken;
(e) Effectiveness of internal control and compliance management systems; and
(f) Financial impact.
4

2.3. Procedures for Imposing Penalty and Timeline
The Authority shall administer the following procedures sequentially and the specified
timeline to identify and impose a monetary penalty and/or administrative sanction(s) on any
individual or FSP.
(a) Identification and Assessment of Violation(s)
(i) The department(s) concerned shall identify the violation(s) through its oversight,
monitoring and other supervisory and surveillance mechanism;
(ii) The department(s) concerned shall document its recommendations and workout
the completed Penalty Matrix (refer to Annexure A) along with the supporting
documents to determine the kind of enforcement action required;
(iii) The department(s) concerned shall complete the Penalty Matrix in accordance
with provisions of Chapter 3 to ensure that the penalty is imposed consistently and
equitably; and
(iv) The findings and recommendations along with the necessary supporting
documents shall be submitted to the Legal Services Division for consultation.
(v) The relevant department, in collaboration with the Legal Services Division, shall
present the matter to the Executive Committee (hereinafter referred to as the
Committee) for the final determination on the imposition of monetary penalty and/or
administrative sanction.
(b) Written Notice
If the Committee decides to impose a penalty (monetary and/or administrative
sanction) on the FSP or an individual, the decision shall be communicated through a
written notice. The written notice, among other things, shall include the following:
(i) Seek explanation for the violation(s) within a 14 working day period in
accordance with Section 157 of the FSA 2011, from the date of issuance of the
notice; and
(ii) Inform the intent of the Authority to impose appropriate penalties stating
specifically the legal and factual grounds upon which it is based.
(iii) Provide an opportunity to submit additional documentary evidence to the
Authority for review and consideration of the penalties as per the timelines set
out.
5

(c) Penalty or No-Penalty Order
Based on the receipt/non-receipt of explanations within 14 working days, the Committee
shall decide the next course of action.
(i) If satisfactory explanations not to impose monetary penalties are furnished, the
Committee may impose any of the administrative sanctions mentioned in Section
2.4. via the Legal Services Division.
(ii) In the event, the Committee is not satisfied with the explanations furnished by
the concerned FSP or the individual, the Authority may impose the following;
a. For FSPs: a Penalty Order specifying the amount, determined based on the
penalty matrix. The Penalty Order may also include corrective actions with
specific timelines for compliance and rectification.
b. For individuals: a monetary penalty not exceeding the equivalent of one
year’s daily minimum wage may be imposed for any violation, subject to the
Authority’s discretion to determine an appropriate amount based on the
factors outlined in Section 2.2. In the case of repeated offenders, the
Authority may impose a monetary penalty and/or administrative sanctions,
and the one year’s daily minimum wage cap shall not necessarily be
applicable.
2.4. Supervisory Powers and Enforcement Actions
The Authority may impose monetary penalty and/or any of the following administrative
sanction on the FSPs and individuals for non-compliance with regulatory requirements,
where applicable, after taking into account the factors outlined in Section 2.2:
(a) Written warnings/letter of advice;
(b) Suspension or revocation of license;
(c) Restriction on business activities or prohibition of specific financial services;
(d) Additional capital charge; or
(e) Any other necessary enforcement measures the Authority deems fit.
2.5. Appeal mechanism
(i) Pursuant to Section 162 of the FSA 2011, the concerned FSP or individual may appeal in
writing to the Authority’s Board within 14 working days from the date on which any
monetary and/or administrative sanction is imposed.
(ii) The Board of the Authority shall affirm, reverse, modify or maintain the status quo of
the decision and state its legal and factual grounds.
(iii) An appeal against the Board’s decision may be filed within 21 working days with a
court of law that has jurisdiction over the FSP or the individual.
6

2.6. Enforcement of Penalty
(i) The penalty imposed on the individual or the FSPs shall be payable to the Authority
within a period of 30 working days from the date of issuing the Penalty Order.
(ii) If the FSP maintains a current account with the Authority, the Department of Banking
shall debit the penalty amount from the FSP’s account upon receiving an order from the
Legal Services Division, provided that the FSP does not file an appeal within 14 working
days.
(iii)The Department of Banking shall maintain a specific account for this purpose.
(iv) For those without an account with the Authority, the penalty may be paid in cash or
through a formal banking channel. Proof of payment must be provided through a receipt,
bank transfer confirmation, or any other verifiable payment instrument, such as a deposit
slip or electronic payment record.
(v) In case of failure in payment of penalty amount, the Authority shall initiate appropriate
action to impose an additional penalty not exceeding twice the amount of the penalty as per
Section 168 of FSA 2011.
2.7. Public Statement
The concerned Department(s) may, following the issuance of a Penalty Order, disclose the
name of the FSP, the amount of the penalty, and the nature of the violation on its official
website or through other appropriate media channels.
CHAPTER 3: PENALTY CALCULATION AND METHODOLOGY
3.1. Number of Matrices
One matrix shall be completed for one FSP for all or one violation. When there are several
violations included in one matrix, the highest severity level applicable for any of them will
be recorded for each factor in the matrix.
3.2. Explanation of the Factors
(a) Concealment: This factor considers the extent to which the violation or relevant
facts were concealed. It includes situations where there was no concealment and
the misconduct was voluntarily self-disclosed; where disclosure occurred only
upon request by the Authority or another relevant body; and where the FSP
actively took steps to conceal the misconduct or material facts from the Authority,
auditors, or other regulatory bodies.
(b) Repetition of violation in the last five years: This factor considers whether the FSP
has committed the same violation within the last five years. It distinguishes
7

between three levels of recurrence: (i) no repetition, where the violation is a
first-time occurrence within the five-year period; (ii) a single repetition, where the
same violation has occurred once within the last five years. Any prior occurrence
outside this five-year window is not considered under this factor, and (iii) multiple
repetitions, where the same violation has been committed more than once within
the same timeframe, indicating a recurring compliance failure or disregard for
regulatory requirements. For example, a previous Capital Adequacy Ratio
requirement violation and a current Capital Adequacy Ratio requirement violation.
(c) Duration and frequency of violation(s) before Written Notice: This factor assesses
the length of time and frequency with which a violation or non-compliant practice
occurred prior to the issuance of a written notice by the Authority. It includes: (i)
isolated violations, where the conduct was infrequent or occurred as a single
instance over a short period; (ii) repeated or sustained violation(s) lasting up to one
year, where the same or similar violation(s) occurred multiple times or were
ongoing for a period not exceeding one year; and (iii) prolonged violation(s)
exceeding one year, where the conduct persisted for more than one year prior to
regulatory detection or intervention, reflecting a sustained failure to comply with
regulatory requirements. Under severity level 2, “practice” includes if the conduct
of violations is prescribed in the FSP’s internal policies and procedures. This factor
does not assess prior resolved violations but focuses solely on the duration and
frequency of the conduct leading up to the current enforcement action.
(d) Continuation after Written Notice: this factor refers to a formal notice issued by the
Authority to the FSP following the Authority’s determination of a violation, or
other non-compliance. Such notification shall set out the particulars of the alleged
contravention and require the FSP to provide an explanation within the period
specified by the Authority.
(e) Impact on financial stability/systemic risk/reputational risk/public service: No
impact means there is no effect on financial stability/systemic risk/reputational risk
or on the public service delivery. An indirect impact suggests secondary effects
through market or institutional connections, while a direct impact poses an
immediate threat, potentially triggering a crisis within the FSP or the entire
financial system.
(f) Financial gain or loss to the FSP as a result of violation: Includes any direct or
indirect monetary gain or loss to the FSP.
8

(g) Impact or harm other than the financial loss to the FSP: Impact or harm other than
financial loss can be any possible negative impact or harm such as increased
reputational risk, operational risk, or compliance risk to the FSP. It can also include
harm to consumers or to the public resulting from the violation(s).
(h) Effectiveness of Internal Controls and compliance management systems: This
factor is to evaluate whether and how the FSP’s internal controls or compliance
programs, or lack thereof, contributed to the violation or deficiency in question.
Internal control systems or compliance management programs that are so lacking
as to permit the violation to occur and remain undetected should be accorded the
most severe score. Internal control systems or compliance programs that identified
the violation or deficiency, which allowed the FSP to initiate timely corrective
measures, may receive a lower score.
CHAPTER 4: MISCELLANEOUS
4.1. Amendment and Review
The Authority reserves the right to amend or review these regulations, including the penalty
matrix, as and when necessary, in response to development in the financial sector and the broader
economy.
4.2. Definitions
In these Regulations, unless the context otherwise requires;
(a) Acts refer to Royal Monetary Authority of Bhutan Act of Bhutan, 2010 and
Financial Services Act of Bhutan, 2011.
(b) Authority means Royal Monetary Authority of Bhutan established under Section 3
of the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan, 2010.
(c) Board means the Board of the Authority established under Section 33 of the Royal
Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan, 2010.
(d) Executive Committee means the Committee established under Section 56 of the
Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan, 2010.
(e) Financial Service Providers means any person engaged in banking business,
insurance business, securities business and all other services designated in a
regulation adopted by the Authority as a financial service.
(f) Person means a natural or a juridical person.
(g) Repeated offender means an individual who has committed the same or a
substantially similar violation on more than one occasion within a five-year period.
